newsitem.title: UK: Euro bourses end sharply off, hit by Wall St.
newsitem.headline: Euro bourses end sharply off, hit by Wall St.

text.p: European bourses closed sharply lower on Monday, dragged down as Wall Street fell on jitters about higher interest rates.

On currency markets, the dollar regained a little poise after losing a pfennig in advance of German figures this week which could signal returning strength to the German economy -- good news for the mark against the dollar.
The weak end to European stocks was in contrast to a strong rally last Friday which saw London, Frankfurt and Paris end with big gains as Wall Street climbed.

European stocks, in the minus column for most of the day, dipped further as the Dow Jones industrials average lost nearly one percent, rattled by interest rate fears and investment guru Warren Buffet's comment that stocks are overvalued.
In London, stocks closed with losses of 1.15 percent, weighed down by Wall Street's negative showing rather than political concerns over the announcement of Britain's general election date, May 1.

Prime Minister John Major ended months of speculation by setting the date but the news failed to set pulses racing in the stock market. Analysts said the election date, and an expected victory for the opposition Labour Party, had already been taken into account by the market.

The London market was depressed by the affect of several big companies going ex-dividend as well as Wall Street -- where investors worried about a possible interest rate hike when the U.S. central bank's policy-making Federal Open Markets Committee (FOMC) meets on March 25.
Joe Rooney, strategist at Lehman Brothers, said the election announcement would have little impact despite the likely win for Labour, traditionally regarded as less friendly to business.
"The election announcement hasn't done anything to the market, we all knew it was coming," one dealer said. "Half the fall is from ex-dividends and the rest is worries about Wall Street."

"Concerns on the U.S. interest rate front are beginning to tell," said David McBain, UK equity strategist at NatWest. "Clearly an increased risk of a pre-emptive move in interest rates is being factored in to share prices."
In Frankfurt, floor trade, which ended before New York opened, lost early gains to close with a modest 0.25 percent loss. But the screen-based IBIS DAX index finished down nearly two percent.
Dealers blamed the falling dollar which dimmed export prospects, adding that speculation about the start of Europe's monetary union added a degree of confusion to a market.
"Markets around Europe are a bit drifty but we don't see any real selling (in the German market)," one trader said.

Speculation had been fuelled about a possible delay to the launch of Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) by an article in the Bild newspaper quoting German finance minister Theo Waigel as saying that adherence to the EMU criteria was more important than the timetable.
Paris was hit badly by the downturn in sentiment and showed losses of more than two percent at the close. Traders said investors were worried about the dollar and volatility of the markets.
The dollar, weak in early trading, recovered composure against the mark and yen in late Europe as bargain-hunters gave the U.S. currency a boost after it drifted to a low of 1.6853 marks.
"(The dollar) went a bit too far. Most people are still bullish on the dollar and looking to buy it on the dips," said Lee Ferridge, currency strategist at Commerzbank.
The main focus this week will be on German economic data which includes the February IFO business climate survey, February M3 money supply and German prices data.
The figures will be watched closely for any sign of returning strength to the German economy which will be mark supportive.

Against the yen, the dollar ended a touch stronger at 123.63. Analysts said a 6.5 percent rise in Japan's February trade surplus, the first in over two years, was widely expected and had little effect on dollar/yen.
"There is little on the news front and the moves at the moment are really consolidative," said a British bank dealer. "The focus is on the German data and U.S. trade numbers this week."
Sterling recovered some ground after Major called the election for May 1, but later sank again to test fresh six-week lows of 2.6795 marks.
CURRENCIES AT 1700 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 1.6901 marks and 123.63 yen, compared with Friday's late European levels of 1.6972 marks and 123.45 yen.
STOCK MARKETS
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index ended down 51.0 points at 4,373.3.
PARIS - The CAC-40 finished down 57.24 points at 2,588.38.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index closed down down 8.3 points at 3,350.99. In scree-based trade the IBIS DAX closed down 67.18 points at 3,337.11.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold closed at $350.25 an ounce, compared with $352.75 at the close on Friday. Silver was at $5.23, compared with $5.31.
